messages.content: Maintain a 2:1 ratio of declarative to interrogative sentences in your response. Show a metric space (M, d) is complete if and only if any sequence (F_n) of nonempty closed subsets of M with - F_{n+1} \subset F_n - diam F_n \rightarrow 0 as n \rightarrow \infty has a nonempty intersection

message.content:
We may assume (M,d) is complete and (F_n) is a nested sequence of nonempty closed sets with F_{n+1} \subset F_n and diam F_n \rightarrow 0.
Does the intersection contain a point?
Let x_n be chosen in F_n; then for m>n both x_n and x_m lie in F_n, and diam F_n \rightarrow 0 makes (x_n) Cauchy, completeness gives x \in M, and the closedness of each F_n forces x into every F_n.
Conversely, how does the intersection property yield completeness?
For a Cauchy sequence (x_k), let F_n be the closure of \{x_k : k \ge n\}; these sets are nonempty closed, nested, and satisfy diam F_n \rightarrow 0, so their intersection is nonempty.
Any point of that intersection is a limit of (x_k), proving (M,d) is complete.
